🗺️ Bad Eden TERRITORY & ECONOMY

How the World Actually Works

1. What a Hex Is (Mechanically)

A hex is not land.
A hex is commitment.

In Bad Eden, a hex is the smallest unit of territory that the game actually reasons about. Every hex tracks:

  • who controls it

  • what it produces

  • how hard it is to hold

  • how much it costs to keep

  • how deeply it is integrated into a faction’s identity

If you want to understand why your faction is rich, broke, powerful, unstable, or collapsing — you start with hexes.

Core Hex Properties (Always Present)

PropertyWhat It Means
OwnerWhich faction controls the hex (or none)
StatusUnclaimed, Occupied, Contested, Scorched
TypeWhat kind of place it is (Farm, Mine, Fortress, etc.)
SizePhysical scale of development
PopulationWho lives there, and how hostile or loyal they are
ResourcesWhat the hex actually produces
IntegrationHow deeply this hex is part of the faction
Modifiers / ConditionsGood things, bad things, scars of history

These values are not flavor. They are read every turn by the economy, logistics, and upkeep systems.

2. Hex Status — Who’s in Control (and How Secure)

StatusMeaning
UnclaimedNo faction control. Produces nothing of value.
OccupiedControlled by force or recent conquest. Expensive to hold.
ContestedActively unstable. Upkeep is high; trouble is likely.
ScorchedDestroyed. No production. Integration blocked.

Player Warning:
Occupied hexes are not “basically yours.”
They are bleeding you every turn until you integrate them.

3. Hex Type — What the Place Is

Hex Type determines the kind of resources a hex is naturally capable of producing.
This is the starting shape of the economy.

Base Resource Output by Hex Type

(before Size, Modifiers, Sephirot, or Conditions)

Hex TypeFoodMaterialsTradeMilitaryKnowledge
FarmHighLowLow——
Mine—HighLow——
Settlement——MediumLow—
Fortress—Medium—High—
PortMediumMediumHigh——
Factory—HighMediumLow—
Research————High
TempleLowLowLow—Medium
Ruins—Low——Low
Wilderness—————

Important:
Wilderness hexes produce nothing until developed.
Expansion without development is a trap.

4. Hex Size — How Big the Place Is

Size multiplies the base output of a hex and increases its defensive footprint.

SizeOutput MultiplierDefense Bonus
Outpost×0.5+0
Village×0.75+1
Town×1.0+1
City×1.5+2
Metropolis×2.0+3
Megalopolis×3.0+4

Mal Says:
Bigger is better only if you can afford it.
Cities are power engines — and upkeep monsters.

5. Modifiers & Conditions — Why Two Farms Are Never Equal

Modifiers are persistent truths about a hex.
They stack, they multiply, and they absolutely matter.

Common Positive Modifiers

ModifierEffect
Well-Maintained+25% all production
Loyal Population+15% production, loyalty boost
Trade Hub+50% Trade output
Strategic Position+10% production
FortifiedMajor defense bonus

Common Negative Modifiers

ModifierEffect
Hostile Population−25% production, unrest risk
Damaged Infrastructure−25% production
Radiation Zone−75% production
Contaminated−50% production
Supply Line Vulnerable−10% production

Conditions (State-Based)

ConditionEffect
RadiatedIncreases upkeep, spreads Darkness
PurifiedReduces upkeep, stabilizes hex
UnstableIncreases risk events

Player Rule of Thumb:
If a hex has two or more negative modifiers, it is probably costing you more than it gives.

6. Sephirotic Alignment — Metaphysics with Math

When a hex is aligned to a Sephirah, it gains flat bonuses on top of all other math.

SephirahPrimary Effect
Keter+1 to all resources
ChokhmahKnowledge & Trade bonus
BinahKnowledge & Trade bonus
ChesedDiplomacy & Loyalty
GevurahMilitary & Defense
TiferetDiplomacy & Loyalty
NetzachMilitary & Momentum
HodKnowledge & Trade
YesodTrade & Diplomacy
MalkuthTrade & Materialization

Alignment is not cosmetic.
Three aligned hexes + an integrated Spark = Unity bonuses every turn.

7. Effective Resources — The Actual Math

Each turn, the game computes Effective Resources like this:

  1. Base output from Type

  2. × Size multiplier

  3. Sephirotic flat bonuses

  4. × Modifiers (good and bad)

  5. Rounded to whole numbers

These effective resources are then used by:

  • OP regeneration

  • Build Unit generation

  • Logistics capacity

  • Faction status calculations

This is why the Hex Sheet matters.
The numbers you see there are the numbers the game uses.

8. From Resources to Power (OP)

Resources do not equal OP directly.

Instead:

  • Resources feed specific OP channels

  • OP regenerates each turn based on:

    • stockpiled resources

    • logistics pressure

    • overextension penalties

Example mappings (simplified):

ResourceFeeds OP Type
FoodLogistics
MaterialsEconomy
TradeDiplomacy
MilitaryViolence
KnowledgeIntrigue

If your logistics are strained, logistics OP regen is reduced, even if you have resources.

Mal Says:
You don’t lose because you lack power.
You lose because you can’t move it.

9. Build Units — Engineering Reality

Build Units (BU) represent industrial and engineering capacity.

What Build Units Are Used For

ActionEffect
Fortify HexAdds Fortified modifier
Repair HexRemoves Damaged Infrastructure
Build AssetsFuture systems

Build Units:

  • are stored on the faction

  • are generated indirectly from materials

  • are finite and precious

Player Advice:
If you are constantly repairing, you are fighting the map instead of shaping it.

10. Integration Track (0–6) — Making It Yours

Integration measures how deeply a hex belongs to a faction.

ProgressStageWhat Changes
0WildNo integration
1–2OutpostMinimal control
3–4DevelopingPopulation stabilizes
5SettledLoyal population possible
6IntegratedFull benefits, low upkeep

Integration affects:

  • upkeep cost

  • morale & loyalty bonuses

  • logistics capacity

  • Unity eligibility

Some outcomes advance integration faster.
Some (like Salt the Earth) reset it completely.

11. Garrison & Upkeep — The Cost of Holding Ground

Every occupied or integrating hex costs OP every turn.

Upkeep is calculated from:

  • hex type

  • size

  • integration phase

  • outcome used to take it

  • population loyalty/hostility

  • conditions (radiation, instability)

What Happens If You Don’t Pay

  • Morale penalties

  • Loyalty loss

  • Darkness increase

  • Hex penalties queued for next turn

What Happens If You Do Pay

  • Integrated hexes grant morale & loyalty bonuses

  • Stable empires become cheaper over time

This is the empire game.
Expansion is easy. Holding is hard.

12. Turn Timing — Why Things Don’t Happen Instantly

Bad Eden runs on turn-based world logic.

Many actions:

  • queue requests

  • resolve on Advance Turn

  • apply consequences one step later

If something “didn’t happen yet,” it’s usually because:

  • it’s queued

  • the world hasn’t advanced

  • or upkeep failed first

13. End-to-End Example (Short)

  1. Claim a wilderness hex → produces nothing

  2. Develop to Outpost → small output, high upkeep

  3. Win a Raid with Justice / Reformation

  4. Integration progresses → population stabilizes

  5. Build infrastructure → modifiers improve output

  6. Align to Sephirah → flat bonuses apply

  7. Fully integrate → upkeep drops, unity possible

That’s the loop.

🚩 Territory Truths to Remember

  • Hexes don’t make you rich — systems do

  • Occupation is a debt, not a prize

  • Integration is the real victory condition

  • Logistics kills more empires than enemies

  • The map always collects what it’s owed

⚖️ Two Factions, One World

A Tale of OP as Energy, Not Currency

The Starting Line (Same for Both)

Both factions begin the campaign the same way:

  • 1 starting hex (Wilderness → Outpost)

  • Low OP reserves

  • No Unity bonuses

  • No integrated Sparks

  • One adjacent wilderness hex

  • Pressure already ticking (Darkness exists in the world)

This matters.
Bad Eden is not a snowball game — it is a pressure game.

🌱 FACTION A: The Verdant Compact

(Well-Managed, Early-Stage Success)

Turn 1 — Listening Before Acting

The Verdant Compact does almost nothing flashy.

They:

  • Spend OP on stabilization, not expansion

  • Develop their starting hex into a Farm

  • Accept low immediate returns

  • Leave the adjacent wilderness alone

Mechanical reality:

  • Their Farm produces Food

  • Food feeds Logistics OP

  • Logistics OP increases capacity, not aggression

Narrative truth:
The Compact believes survival comes before conquest.

OP here is not “spent” — it is allowed to circulate.

Turn 2 — Energy Finds a Shape

They:

  • Pay garrison upkeep in full

  • Avoid Hostile Population

  • Gain no penalties, no drama

Their OP regen is modest but clean.

What the math is doing:

  • No unpaid upkeep → no morale loss

  • No Darkness increase

  • Logistics pressure stays stable

  • OP regen flows unblocked

Narrative truth:
Nothing explodes. That’s the point.

In Bad Eden, nothing going wrong is already a victory.

Turn 3 — The First Choice That Matters

They take the adjacent hex — but carefully.

  • A Raid with Justice / Reformation

  • Accept slower integration in exchange for stability

Mechanical effects:

  • Loyal Population replaces Hostile

  • Integration progresses to Outpost

  • Upkeep multiplier is reduced

  • Morale and Loyalty both tick up

Narrative truth:
The people don’t resist because the Compact doesn’t treat them like fuel.

OP here is relational energy — belief turning into capacity.

Turn 5 — Quiet Power

Now the Compact controls:

  • 2 hexes

  • Both partially integrated

  • Both paying upkeep without stress

They:

  • Spend Build Units to Repair instead of Fortify

  • Delay militarization

  • Align one hex to Chesed

What happens mechanically:

  • Loyalty modifiers increase output

  • Upkeep costs shrink as integration deepens

  • OP regen increases without raising demand

Narrative truth:
Power arrives without announcement.

By Turn 6:

  • They qualify for Unity

  • Their OP feels heavier — each point does more work

Outcome: Living Territory

The Verdant Compact:

  • Has fewer hexes

  • But more usable OP

  • Higher morale

  • Lower Darkness

  • Fewer emergencies

They didn’t win by grabbing energy.
They won by letting it settle.

🔥 FACTION B: The Iron Mandate

(Poorly Managed, Early Collapse)

Same start. Same map. Same rules.

Different instincts.

Turn 1 — Motion Equals Success (They Think)

The Iron Mandate:

  • Immediately raids the adjacent hex

  • Chooses Retribution / Subjugation

  • Ignores integration costs

Mechanical consequences:

  • Hostile Population

  • Higher upkeep

  • Production penalty

  • Darkness increases

Narrative truth:
Fear moves fast. It also leaks.

OP is treated as ammunition, not circulation.

Turn 2 — Debt Disguised as Power

They:

  • Spend OP on Fortify

  • Skip repairs

  • Miss part of garrison upkeep

What the system does:

  • Partial upkeep → Morale loss

  • Loyalty drops

  • Darkness ticks upward

  • Future OP regen is reduced

Narrative truth:
The Mandate believes they are feared.
The world believes they are unstable.

OP now has resistance — energy is lost as heat.

Turn 3 — Chasing the Leak

They expand again to compensate.

  • Another Raid

  • Another Occupied hex

  • Another Hostile Population

Now:

  • Logistics demand spikes

  • Overextension penalty triggers

  • Logistics OP regen is reduced

Narrative truth:
Every victory requires a larger victory to justify it.

The math is screaming, quietly.

Turn 4 — The Spiral

They cannot:

  • Pay full upkeep

  • Repair infrastructure

  • Reduce hostility

System outcomes:

  • Morale penalties stack

  • Loyalty collapses

  • Darkness increases again

  • Integration stalls at 0–1

OP still exists — but it’s trapped energy.

Turn 6 — Collapse Without a Battle

No enemy finishes them.

Instead:

  • Hex penalties queue

  • Production falls

  • Upkeep costs exceed regen

  • Faction status degrades

Narrative truth:
The Iron Mandate didn’t lose a war.
They lost coherence.

🧠 What This Teaches (Explicitly)

OP Is Not Money

Money is inert.
OP is potential.

  • If it circulates → stability

  • If it pools → power

  • If it leaks → collapse

Territory Is a Capacitor

Hexes store, resist, or amplify OP.

  • Integrated hexes smooth flow

  • Occupied hexes add friction

  • Scorched hexes bleed energy

Violence Is Expensive Later

Bad Eden doesn’t punish aggression immediately.
It punishes it after the adrenaline fades.

🜂 The Metaphysical Layer (The Nuance You Mentioned)

OP is not abstract.

In-fiction, OP is:

  • belief

  • trust

  • logistics

  • coordination

  • myth made actionable

A faction with high OP doesn’t “have more stuff.”
They have less resistance between intent and reality.

That’s why:

  • Unity matters

  • Integration matters

  • Loyalty multiplies output

  • Darkness eats capacity, not numbers

🎭 Final Contrast (One Sentence Each)

The Verdant Compact

“We did not conquer the land. We taught it to breathe with us.”

The Iron Mandate

“We ruled everything — until nothing answered us.”

⚙️ Bad Eden OP ENGINE & FACTION ECONOMY

Power Is Not What You Have — It’s What You Can Move

1. What OP Actually Is

OP is not money.
OP is not mana.
OP is energy that can become action.

In Bad Eden, Operations Points (OP) represent a faction’s ability to translate intent into reality.

That translation can take many forms:

  • violence

  • diplomacy

  • logistics

  • intrigue

  • cultural pressure

  • faith

  • coordination

OP is potential difference.
When there’s no difference, nothing moves.

Core Truth (Players Should Memorize This)

OP does not measure strength.
OP measures flow.

A faction with:

  • high OP but bad logistics = stalled

  • low OP but high unity = dangerous

  • balanced OP + integration = inevitable

2. OP Is Channelized (Not a Single Pool)

OP exists in channels, each representing a different way power expresses itself.

Core OP Channels

OP ChannelWhat It Represents
ViolenceMilitary force, raids, coercion
NonlethalCrowd control, restraint, capture
IntrigueEspionage, secrets, manipulation
EconomyProduction, construction, markets
DiplomacyTreaties, alliances, leverage
LogisticsSupply, travel, upkeep capacity
CultureMyth, morale, shared identity
FaithRitual power, metaphysical authority

You don’t “convert” OP freely.
You choose which muscles your faction has trained.

3. Where OP Comes From

OP is generated, not granted.

Primary OP Sources

SourceWhat It Does
TerritoryFeeds OP via effective resources
IntegrationReduces upkeep, improves net gain
Unity BonusesFlat OP deltas or cap increases
FacilitiesDirect, predictable OP income
Roster ContributionsCharacters feeding faction OP
Narrative BeatsOne-time OP injections

If you don’t know why your OP changed, check your War Logs.
The system always tells you.

4. OP Regeneration — The Quiet Turn

Every strategic turn, OP regeneration happens after territory effects and before upkeep penalties fully land.

Simplified Regen Flow

  1. Effective resources are totaled

  2. Resources map into OP channels

  3. Logistics pressure is calculated

  4. Overextension reduces regen

  5. Unity bonuses apply

  6. OP is added to the faction bank

Important:
You can be resource-rich and OP-poor if logistics are strained.

Example Mapping (Simplified)

ResourceFeeds OP Channel
FoodLogistics
MaterialsEconomy
TradeDiplomacy
MilitaryViolence
KnowledgeIntrigue

This mapping can be modified by:

  • faction traits

  • enlightenment

  • story effects

  • GM overrides

5. Logistics Pressure — Why Empires Choke

Logistics is the hidden governor of the OP engine.

Logistics pressure increases with:

  • number of hexes

  • distance from core territory

  • occupation & partial integration

  • active rigs

  • sprawl beyond capacity

Overextension Bands (Player-Facing)

BandEffect
StableNo penalty
StretchedWarning only
Overextended−10% Logistics OP regen
Strained−20% Logistics OP regen
Critical−35% Logistics OP regen

This is how Bad Eden prevents snowballing without hard caps.

6. OP Caps — Why Unity Matters

Every OP channel has a soft cap.

If regen would exceed the cap:

  • excess OP is lost

  • unless Unity or effects temporarily raise the cap

Unity bonuses can:

  • increase caps

  • increase regen

  • or do both

Mal Says:
Power without coherence spills.

7. Spending OP — Action Is Lossy

Every time you spend OP, you are:

  • collapsing potential into reality

  • increasing friction elsewhere

Common OP Sinks

ActionOP Cost Shape
RaidsHigh, spiky
TravelLogistics-heavy
Garrison UpkeepPersistent drain
IntegrationSlow, steady
RepairsEconomy-heavy
RitualsFaith-heavy

A good faction doesn’t avoid spending OP.
They avoid spending it twice.

8. Faction Economy ≠ OP Bank

This is subtle but crucial.

EconomyOP
Long-termTurn-to-turn
StructuralTactical
SlowFast
Shapes capacityShapes action

Territory builds economy.
Economy feeds OP.
OP expresses will.

If you burn OP without growing economy, you collapse.
If you grow economy without spending OP, you stagnate.

9. Story Pair: Flow vs Hoarding

🟢 Faction C: The Luminous Exchange (Good Economy)

They:

  • Invest in Ports and Trade Hubs

  • Keep Logistics OP healthy

  • Spend OP every turn, but never all of it

Result:

  • OP regen stays flat even as territory grows

  • Unity bonuses raise caps just in time

  • No turn feels desperate

Narrative truth:
Their power arrives when needed, not before.

🔴 Faction D: The Gilded Vault (Bad Economy)

They:

  • Hoard OP

  • Avoid integration

  • Delay upkeep “until later”

Result:

  • OP caps overflow → wasted regen

  • Logistics collapses suddenly

  • Multiple penalties land in one turn

Narrative truth:
Stored power rots if it never moves.

10. Reading Your Own Economy (Player Checklist)

Ask these every turn:

  • Which OP channel am I starved for?

  • Is logistics limiting me?

  • Are caps causing waste?

  • Is my territory paying for itself yet?

  • Am I spending OP to fix problems or to create them?

If you can answer those, you’re playing Bad Eden correctly.

🜂 Final Truth

OP is not power.
OP is the speed at which belief becomes consequence.

Territory stores it.
Unity shapes it.
Logistics governs it.
And the turn engine decides whether it flows — or breaks.

Power Is What You Give Up

In Bad Eden, power is not created.
It is redirected.

The OP transference system allows certain forms of mechanical depletion to be converted into faction-level momentum. This is not free power. This is burning potential to force reality to move now.

1. Valid Transference Fuels

OP can be generated by converting personal or structural strain into faction-scale action. The system recognizes the following fuels:

🩸 Integrity (Physical Vitality)

(Previously covered)

  • Represents blood, injury, and bodily sacrifice

  • Immediate, dangerous, and visible

  • Leaves lasting narrative scars

Integrity → OP is the most primal form of transference.

🔮 Clarity points (Arcane & Mystical Capacity)

Clarity points are stored possibility.

When a Clarity points is burned for OP:

  • The caster gives up future certainty

  • The faction gains immediate coordination

What this represents in-fiction:

  • manifestations uncast

  • rituals aborted

  • destinies narrowed

  • the mage choosing the world over the self

A Clarity points spent this way is not “used.”
It is unlived.

Design intent:

  • High-impact, limited use

  • Excellent for clutch turns

  • Strong thematic weight for ritual-heavy factions

🧠 Stress Levels (Systemic Strain)

Stress is structural failure in motion.

When Stress is converted to OP:

  • the character is not hurt

  • the system is not broken

  • but resilience is eroded

What this means narratively:

  • sleepless nights

  • fraying discipline

  • leaders making decisions on fumes

  • systems running without slack

Stress is what happens when victory comes too fast.

This form of transference is especially potent for:

  • siege scenarios

  • long campaigns

  • factions under sustained pressure

🎲 Pool Dice (Momentum & Narrative Capital)

Pool dice represent:

  • readiness

  • narrative leverage

  • latent advantage

Converting pool dice into OP means:

  • you collapse probability

  • you sacrifice flexibility for certainty

  • you choose now over later

In-fiction framing:

  • calling in favors

  • burning goodwill

  • revealing secrets

  • exhausting contingency plans

Pool dice are hope.
Spending them is choosing which future survives.

2. What All Transference Has in Common

No matter the fuel, all transference shares three traits:

1. It Is Lossy

Something is always permanently diminished.

2. It Is Logged

Every transference:

  • appears in War Logs

  • is visible to the system

  • becomes part of the faction’s story

3. It Has Consequences

Transference:

  • increases momentum

  • but reduces long-term stability

  • and often attracts Darkness, Attention, or Debt

You can always tell a faction that relies on transference.
They move fast.
They burn bright.
They do not last without reform.

3. Choosing the Right Fuel (Player Guidance)

FuelBest Used When
IntegrityDesperation, martyrdom, last stands
Clarity pointsRitual turns, metaphysical stakes
StressSustained crisis, siege conditions
Pool DiceNarrative pivots, decisive gambits

A healthy faction:

  • uses transference sparingly

  • plans recovery afterward

  • understands the cost before paying it

An unhealthy faction:

  • treats transference as income

  • stacks depletion

  • collapses when recovery is needed most

🜂 Final Metaphysical Truth

OP is not powered by strength.
It is powered by what you are willing to lose.

Land stores it.
Unity shapes it.
Logistics governs it.

But transference?
Transference is when a faction decides the future is worth bleeding for right now.

Every OP channel has a soft cap.

If regen would exceed the cap:

Unity bonuses can:

  • increase regen

  • or do both

OP is not power.

Power Is What You Give Up

In Bad Eden, power is not created.
It is redirected.

The OP transference system allows certain forms of mechanical depletion to be converted into faction-level momentum. This is not free power. This is burning potential to force reality to move now.

1. Valid Transference Fuels

OP can be generated by converting personal or structural strain into faction-scale action. The system recognizes the following fuels:

🩸 Integrity (Physical Vitality)

(Previously covered)

  • Represents blood, injury, and bodily sacrifice

  • Immediate, dangerous, and visible

  • Leaves lasting narrative scars

Integrity → OP is the most primal form of transference.

🔮 Clarity points (Arcane & Mystical Capacity)

Clarity points are stored possibility.

When a Clarity points is burned for OP:

  • The caster gives up future certainty

  • The faction gains immediate coordination

What this represents in-fiction:

  • manifestations uncast

  • rituals aborted

  • destinies narrowed

  • the mage choosing the world over the self

A Clarity points spent this way is not “used.”
It is unlived.

Design intent:

  • High-impact, limited use

  • Excellent for clutch turns

  • Strong thematic weight for ritual-heavy factions

🧠 Stress Levels (Systemic Strain)

Stress is structural failure in motion.

When Stress is converted to OP:

  • the character is not hurt

  • the system is not broken

  • but resilience is eroded

What this means narratively:

  • sleepless nights

  • fraying discipline

  • leaders making decisions on fumes

  • systems running without slack

Stress is what happens when victory comes too fast.

This form of transference is especially potent for:

  • siege scenarios

  • long campaigns

  • factions under sustained pressure

🎲 Pool Dice (Momentum & Narrative Capital)

Pool dice represent:

  • readiness

  • narrative leverage

  • latent advantage

Converting pool dice into OP means:

  • you collapse probability

  • you sacrifice flexibility for certainty

  • you choose now over later

In-fiction framing:

  • calling in favors

  • burning goodwill

  • revealing secrets

  • exhausting contingency plans

Pool dice are hope.
Spending them is choosing which future survives.

2. What All Transference Has in Common

No matter the fuel, all transference shares three traits:

1. It Is Lossy

Something is always permanently diminished.

2. It Is Logged

Every transference:

  • appears in War Logs

  • is visible to the system

  • becomes part of the faction’s story

3. It Has Consequences

Transference:

  • increases momentum

  • but reduces long-term stability

  • and often attracts Darkness, Attention, or Debt

You can always tell a faction that relies on transference.
They move fast.
They burn bright.
They do not last without reform.

3. Choosing the Right Fuel (Player Guidance)

FuelBest Used When
IntegrityDesperation, martyrdom, last stands
Clarity pointsRitual turns, metaphysical stakes
StressSustained crisis, siege conditions
Pool DiceNarrative pivots, decisive gambits

A healthy faction:

  • uses transference sparingly

  • plans recovery afterward

  • understands the cost before paying it

An unhealthy faction:

  • treats transference as income

  • stacks depletion

  • collapses when recovery is needed most

🜂 Final Metaphysical Truth

OP is not powered by strength.
It is powered by what you are willing to lose.

Land stores it.
Unity shapes it.
Logistics governs it.

But transference?
Transference is when a faction decides the future is worth bleeding for right now.
